entries.seminar_title: Managerial Experience, Firm Size, and Economic Development: Evidence from Japan’s Decolonization
entries.speaker: Shizuka Inoue
entries.abstract: I study how the scarcity of workers with managerial experience limits firm size and economic development, combining evidence from a natural experiment with a quantitative model. After World War II, three million Japanese civilians, many of them with managerial experience, were forced to return to Japan. I use repatriates' historical family ties to Japanese districts to isolate exogenous variation in local inflows of workers with managerial experience. The inflow shifted employment from self-employment toward wage work and from agriculture toward manufacturing and services. Firms grew larger, expanded beyond their headquarters cities, and participated more in overseas programs teaching modern U.S. management practices. I develop a spatial model in which managerial experience expands the pool of workers qualified for management. Managers supervise production within establishments and implement practices that raise productivity across the firm's establishment network. Removing the managerial experience of these repatriates lowers aggregate output per worker by 4 percent. Firms' geographic expansion accounts for about a quarter of this effect, amplifying the aggregate impact from managerial experience.

entries.seminar_title: Ecological Imperialism: Climate and the Demographic Success of European Settlement
entries.speaker: Marco Tabellini
entries.abstract: Since 1500, millions of Europeans settled overseas, and by 2000 nearly half of all people of European descent lived outside Europe. Yet, the scale and persistence of European settlement varied dramatically across destinations. What explains where Europeans settled overseas and why some settler populations expanded while others did not? We test Alfred Crosby's Ecological Imperialism hypothesis that ecological compatibility between Europe and overseas territories shaped the demographic success of European settlement. We combine genealogical microdata on more than 290,000 Europeans born between 1500 and 1850 who died outside Europe with high-resolution climate and agronomic data to measure ecological similarity between settlers' origins and destinations. We first show that both temperature and agronomic distance reduced permanent European settlement. We then document that temperature, but not agronomic, distance also reduced settlers' longevity and fertility. Finally, we show that locations where European settlers faced greater temperature and agronomic distance have lower agricultural output today, even within countries. Temperature distance further predicts lower nighttime luminosity, suggesting that its relationship with long-run development extended beyond agriculture, whereas agronomic distance was related only to agricultural output.
